headline: Chips Surge as Broader Market Retreats; Geopolitical Tensions Set the Tone for the Week Ahead
body_html:
Friday's session closed on a bifurcated note, with semiconductors the lone sector in positive territory as 340 names across the 545-stock universe declined against just 204 advancing. Memory and equipment names led the charge: Sandisk surged nearly 11%, Lam Research and Applied Materials each climbed roughly 7%, and optical-networking specialist Coherent added 7.2%, underscoring a concentrated rally in hardware tied to data-infrastructure demand rather than any broad risk-on sentiment.

The rest of the tape told a different story. Homebuilders bore the steepest losses at -1.6%, with Software, Materials, and Energy each shedding roughly 1%. Steel maker Nucor and metallurgical coal producer Alpha Metallurgical Resources both fell more than 5.5%, reflecting renewed pressure on industrial commodities. Qualcomm's 5.8% drop stood out as the sole semiconductor-sector decliner of consequence, a reminder that not every chip name shared in Friday's rally.

Heading into the new week, the geopolitical backdrop demands attention. Washington signed sweeping Russia sanctions legislation granting broad new tariff authority, while regional tensions around the Iran conflict continue to simmer — factors likely to keep energy and materials markets volatile. Investors will be navigating a complex macro environment as they assess sector rotation signals from Friday's unusual divergence.

briefs.headline: Russia Sanctions Law Expands White House Trade Leverage
briefs.body: President Trump signed landmark Russia sanctions legislation over the weekend, a bill that grants the executive branch expansive new tariff powers beyond the sanctions themselves. Markets will be watching closely for any early signals on how and when those powers might be deployed, with trade-sensitive industrials and materials sectors most directly in the crosshairs.

briefs.headline: Iran-War Casualty Discrepancy Deepens Congressional Scrutiny
briefs.body: A Washington Post investigation reported that U.S. troop deaths during the Iran conflict exceed the Pentagon's official count by at least four, a finding that is expected to intensify oversight hearings on Capitol Hill. The revelation adds a layer of political uncertainty as lawmakers simultaneously debate the scope of sanctions and military posture in the region.

briefs.headline: Riyadh Airport Incident Rattles Gulf Risk Sentiment
briefs.body: Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense issued and subsequently lifted alerts covering several areas near Riyadh after smoke was observed close to the capital's main airport. The episode, coming amid the broader Iran conflict, is a reminder of the tail risk embedded in Middle East energy infrastructure and could keep a floor under crude volatility through the early part of the week.

briefs.headline: Turkey Shutters Iran's Mellat Bank Under U.S. Pressure
briefs.body: Ankara revoked the operating license of Iran's Mellat Bank, a move attributed to alignment with U.S.-led financial measures. The decision narrows Iran's remaining banking conduits in a NATO-member country and signals that secondary-sanctions enforcement is tightening in ways that could affect emerging-market currency flows tied to the region.

briefs.headline: House China Committee Pushes for Harder Line Ahead of Xi Talks
briefs.body: The Republican chair of the House Select Committee on China urged the Trump administration to adopt a more confrontational posture before any high-level meeting with President Xi. The call adds pressure to an already fraught trade relationship and keeps semiconductor-export-control risk on the table just as chip stocks are attempting a leadership rotation.

briefs.headline: Air France Leans Into Luxury as War Disrupts Conventional Routes
briefs.body: Air France has accelerated a premium-cabin strategy, with caviar-and-champagne service upgrades helping the carrier offset the revenue hit from Iran-war-related route restrictions. The pivot illustrates how global travel operators are reshuffling capacity toward high-yield passengers while conventional tourist-market demand remains constrained by regional instability.
